To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) the temporal complexity of a video is typically much less than its spatial resolution, and (ii) this observation can be used to develop efficient algorithms for reconstructing videos using streaming compressive measurements, and (iii) we propose a multiscale reconstruction method that leverages these observations and is shown to produce accurate estimates of the video signal.
(1) the spatial lowpass nature of typical cameras limits the temporal bandwidth of many videos, and that (2) this fact can be exploited to design efficient algorithms for reconstructing videos.

(a) streaming video reconstruction can be performed at a rate that is much slower than that of the measurements, and that (b) the temporal bandwidth of videos is limited by the speed of moving objects, the spatial resolution of imaging sensors, and the temporal complexity of objects in the video.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the problem of reconstructing videos from compressive measurements that are acquired in a streaming manner.
the following question: given a video stream with compressive measurements, can we reconstruct the video at a lower temporal sampling rate?

the following question: how can we reconstruct a video signal from a stream of compressive measurements, where the measurements are acquired by a camera that is moving relative to a scene that may be changing?
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
this paper presents a multiscale algorithm for video reconstruction from compressive measurements.

the proposed algorithm is able to recover videos from streaming compressions measurements, and that it does so with a complexity that depends on the temporal complexity of a video and not on the number of measurements.
our multiscale algorithm is a new and efficient approach for reconstructing video from streaming compressive data.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we propose a multiscale reconstruction framework for videos that exploits the low temporal bandwidth that should be present in many video streams.
the proposed multiscale algorithm can reconstruct videos from streaming compressively sampled data at rates that are orders of magnitude less than the streaming rate.
we present a multiscale, streaming, video reconstruction algorithm that exploits the limited temporal bandwidth of videos.
The main takeaway from our work is that
streaming compressive measurements can be processed at a much lower rate than the sampling rate of the measurements themselves.

, even though streaming video measurements may be taken thousands of times per frame, the complexity of the underlying video may only require reconstructing a few frames per second, which can be done with much lower data rates.
, for a large class of videos, the temporal bandwidth of a video should be much smaller than the temporal rate of the measurement system.
